html:
After the Korean kingdom of Baekje fell, thousands of its nobles, soldiers, monks and craftsmen fled across the sea to Japan in the 660s.

Baekje had been Japan's closest ally on the peninsula, and the source of much of its Buddhism and learning. In 660 Silla and Tang China conquered it. Japan sent a large fleet to help Baekje loyalists restore it, but Tang and Silla forces destroyed it at the Battle of Baekgang in 663. The loyalist cause collapsed, and many fled with the beaten Japanese.

The court settled them in the provinces and put them to work. Fearing a Tang invasion, Japan had Baekje engineers build stone mountain forts in Kyushu and western Japan, in Korean style. Others served as officials, scholars and temple builders, and helped shape the new state of the Taika era and Nara Japan. Many Japanese families trace their ancestry to them.
sum: After the Korean kingdom of Baekje fell, thousands of its nobles, soldiers, monks and craftsmen fled across the sea to Japan in the 660s.
